_why: Four routes answer a Redis outage four DIFFERENT ways, on purpose. Nothing in tests/ records that, so a well-meaning refactor that harmonises them is invisible — and harmonising /scan-url to /event's fail-open is precisely the defect that shipped on 2026-09-18 and was reported as closed while still open. Each row is the answer the route's own header comment promises. Change a row here only when the route's documented posture actually changes, and say why in the note.
_conditions: REDIS_URL points at a closed loopback port, so getRedisStatus() is 'backoff': Redis is EXPECTED and unreachable. This is not the same as REDIS_URL being unset ('disabled'), which is documented local-dev degradation and is covered by the control row in the check.

rows.note: MUST fail closed. The single-use claim IS the replay control, so anyone who can knock Redis over — including by flooding it — would otherwise also switch off single-use, and one solved token buys unlimited scans for its whole 90s life. Redis is on localhost; if it is down the tool is degraded anyway, so refusing is honest rather than costly.

Fails open on purpose. These are cookieless click counters; a page must never wait on analytics, and losing a count costs nothing. 'stored: false' is the honest part — it does not claim to have stored anything.

The id is still issued so the browser can run its probes, and storage:'none' tells the UI to show 'backend not configured' rather than a verdict it cannot support. No security control depends on this write.

Owner-facing. Returning counts:{} with storage:'none' is how the owner can tell an outage from a genuinely quiet day; a bare zero would lie. The bearer check has already run by this point, so nothing is exposed.
